name: Chloe Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Chloe, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a graphic designer at Inkwell, a six-person agency above a bike shop on Mercer Street, and most of our work is posters, flyers and programmes for theatres, galleries and charities. I get in around nine, check what Rosa, my boss, has put on the whiteboard, and then it's layouts in InDesign until lunch. The best bit is when I get to hand-letter a title and scan it in, because that's the part nobody else in the studio does. What wears me out is the third round of changes from a client who just wants the logo bigger.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, who's at home with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My girlfriend Noor, she's a nurse on nights at the city hospital, so we pass each other in the kitchen a lot. We rent a small flat, and I've got about four months of rent and bills saved, which feels okay but not huge. I've never touched any of the AI design tools, and honestly I'd rather keep it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. I'd post something like, see, people still want a human who understands a theatre's audience, not a machine spitting out templates. At work I'd probably tease Rosa, because she bought a subscription to one of those image tools last spring and barely used it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but I'd still be watching the budgets. Our charity clients have been cutting their print runs for two years, and that has nothing to do with AI. If the small routine stuff, like resizing a poster for six social media formats, goes to software, that's a chunk of my week, and I don't know if Rosa fills it with better work or fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and push harder on the hand-lettering side, because that's the thing that makes me hard to swap out. I'd put another fifty a month into savings, since our rent goes up again in March. And I'd keep going to the arts workers' group meetings at the community centre, because pay at small studios is a fight whether AI is involved or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly a relief, like a storm went round us. But it's a tired kind of relief, because the money side of the job was already tight before any of this. I still check the agency's client list in my head every January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said resizing goes to software. What does that look like on an ordinary Tuesday for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now Tuesday is the day I take one poster and make the Instagram square, the story, the banner and the newsletter header, and it eats about three hours. If a tool does that, I either get three hours of real design or Rosa decides she needs me four days a week. I'd honestly rather do the boring resizing than lose a day's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel, the other mid-level designer, because we eat lunch on the fire escape most days. He's the one who'd hear first if Rosa was thinking about hours. Then Noor, because she'd ask straight away what it means for the rent.

say: I'd say **people still want** a designer who understands a theatre's audience, not a template machine.
I'd tease my boss, who **bought an AI subscription** last spring and barely used it.
think: The **charity budgets** were shrinking before AI and will keep shrinking anyway.
If **resizing work** goes to software, my boss might cut my hours instead of giving me better work.
do: Push the **hand-lettering** side of my work so I'm harder to replace.
Add **fifty a month** to savings before the March rent rise.
Keep going to the **arts workers' group** at the community centre.
feel: **Relieved**, but tired, because money in small studios was already **tight**.
S0.quote: I'd honestly rather do the boring resizing than lose a day's pay.
fieldNote: Even in the mildest world she worries about **hours**, because her studio's clients are cash-strapped charities.
Her protection plan is **craft**, not tools: hand-lettering is the skill she thinks nobody can copy.
She frames pay as a **collective** fight, tying her worries to the arts workers' group rather than to AI.

steps.text: Hand-letter more poster titles and show them in her portfolio
Add fifty a month to savings before the March rent rise
Attend the monthly arts workers' group meeting at the community centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loudly: this is a choice companies are making, not the weather. I'd share every story about studios cutting juniors and say we need rules on who owns the work these tools were trained on. At work I'd be the one asking Rosa in the Monday meeting what her plan is for us, not just for the clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think a lot of what I do is exactly the thinking work on that card. Layouts, picking fonts, writing the little bits of copy on a flyer, all of it. If clients can type in what they want and get something decent, the charities will take decent because they're broke. I think Inkwell goes from six to three, and I'm not sure I'm in the three, because I won't use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by asking for my hours in writing, and I'd join the designers' union branch properly instead of just going to meetings. I'd go back to the print workshop on Canal Lane on Saturdays and learn screen printing, because physical posters are the one thing a screen can't hand over. And I'd stop buying anything that isn't rent, food or bills, so my four months could stretch to six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly, and angry under it. It's the feeling of being told the thing you trained for is a hobby now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use the tools. Even if that's what keeps you in the three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it sounds stubborn. Every time I've opened one of those image generators, it feels like it's built out of other artists' work without asking them. I might end up having to, but I'd want a union deal on how it's used before I touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the studio's going to shrink and I might be on the wrong side of it. She'd say her ward is short of staff and they'd hire me as a porter tomorrow, which is sweet and also terrifying. Then we'd sit down with the bank app and work out how long four months really lasts if it's only her pay.

say: I'd say this is a **choice companies are making**, not the weather.
I'd push for **rules on who owns** the work these tools were trained on.
I'd ask my boss in the Monday meeting what her **plan is for staff**.
think: Layouts, fonts and flyer copy are **exactly the work** on that card.
I think my studio shrinks from **six to three**, and I might not be kept.
do: Join the **designers' union branch** properly and ask for my hours in writing.
Learn **screen printing** on Saturdays at the Canal Lane workshop.
Cut spending to rent, food and bills so **four months** stretches to six.
feel: **Scared** that my training gets treated like a hobby.
**Angry** underneath, because it feels like a choice made by companies.
S1.quote: If clients can type in what they want and get something decent, the charities will take decent because they're broke.
fieldNote: Her refusal to use AI is **ethical**, not technical: she objects to tools built on artists' unpaid work.
She expects to be cut because she **won't adapt**, and says so plainly.
Her girlfriend's hospital job is the **household backstop**, which both comforts and frightens her.

steps.text: Join the designers' union branch and ask for her hours in writing
Learn screen printing on Saturdays at the Canal Lane print workshop
Cut spending to rent, food and bills only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments let this happen and they need to catch the people falling through. I'd be out at whatever protest there was, with a hand-lettered sign, obviously. Online I'd be the friend posting about pay for everyone whose job just vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone within a year of 2028. Design is nearly all thinking work, there's barely a hands-on part to hide in. The only bit of me that lasts is the printing and painting, and that's three years until the robots, which is something but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd move every spare pound into savings and stop going out. I'd do the screen printing course and start selling prints at the Sunday market, because a person-made poster might still mean something to some buyers. Once it actually lands, I'd sign on for whatever support there is and push the union to fight for a wage for displaced workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. Two years isn't long enough to become anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the 3 years before robots change what you aim for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'd aim for the hands-on end, printing, sign painting, maybe helping at the print workshop, because that buys me until 2031. But I'm not kidding myself that a market stall pays the rent in a city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Noor's ward. Does her job feel safer in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than mine, for a while, because someone has to turn patients and change dressings. The charting and the rota are thinking work though, so she'd change too. We'd basically be living on her pay and hoping the robots are slow.

say: I'd say **governments let this happen** and must catch the people falling through.
I'd join any **protest** with a hand-lettered sign and post about **pay for everyone**.
think: My design job is **gone within a year** of 2028, since it's almost all thinking work.
Printing and painting give me **three more years**, which is something but not much.
do: Put every spare pound into **savings** and stop going out, starting now.
Sell **screen prints** at the Sunday market once the course is done.
Sign on for **public support** and push the union for a wage for displaced workers.
feel: Like the **floor's gone**, because two years is too short to become anything else.
S2.quote: Design is nearly all thinking work, there's barely a hands-on part to hide in.
fieldNote: She clearly sees the **gap** between thinking AI and robots and aims for the hands-on end of print.
She expects to rely on her **girlfriend's pay**, while knowing nursing also has thinking parts.
Her answer to collapse is **political**: protest, union and a wage for displaced workers.

steps.text: Move every spare pound into savings and stop nights out
Sell hand-pulled screen prints at the Sunday market
Sign on for public support once her design job ends
March with the union for a wage for displaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, just with more time to shout about it. I'd say five years is enough warning that there's no excuse for governments not to have a plan. I'd be the one making the posters for the campaign, ironically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years means I'd watch the studio thin out year by year instead of all at once. Daniel would go first, then me, or the other way round. I'd have time to get properly good at printing, but the design job still ends around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years doing a proper part-time course in printmaking and sign painting, paid out of savings and a bit of overtime. I'd keep my design job as long as Rosa keeps me. And I'd go to every union meeting where they're writing up demands, because five years is time to win something if people organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less like falling, more like watching a slow tide come in. I hate it, but at least I can plan the steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said time to win something. What would winning look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winning would be a law that says if a company replaces you with AI, it pays into a fund that retrains you and keeps your rent paid while you learn. Plus credit for artists whose work trained these things. Small, practical stuff, not a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if nothing like that passes by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm a sign painter with a few clients and a girlfriend on night shifts. I'd probably move somewhere cheaper, maybe back near my mum's town where the rent is half. I don't want to, but I'd rather that than be broke here.

say: I'd say **five years of warning** leaves governments no excuse for having no plan.
I'd make the **campaign posters** myself, which I know is a bit ironic.
think: The studio would **thin out** year by year, and my job still ends around 2031.
Five years is enough to get **properly good** at printing.
do: Take a **part-time course** in printmaking and sign painting, paid from savings and overtime.
Keep my design job **as long as** my boss keeps me.
Help the union write up **demands**, because there's time to win something.
feel: Like watching a **slow tide** come in: I hate it, but I can **plan**.
S3.quote: If a company replaces you with AI, it pays into a fund that retrains you and keeps your rent paid while you learn.
fieldNote: More time turns her from **protest** to organising for a concrete **retraining fund**.
She still expects her design job to **end**, so her mood barely changes from the fast case.
Moving to her **mum's cheaper town** is her quiet fallback, said reluctantly.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time printmaking and sign-painting course
Help the union draft a retraining-fund demand
Look at flats near her mum's town where rent is half

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, so let's use it to make the rules now. I'd be pushing the union to treat it like a slow emergency, not a distant one. And I'd say artists have to be at the table when the rules get written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is my whole late twenties and thirties. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, which is young enough to build a second trade properly. I'd still lose design, I think, but I wouldn't be starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep designing at Inkwell for a good few years and build the printing and sign painting on the side, slowly, with real clients. I'd try to save up to six months, and maybe go in with two friends on a shared print studio. I'd keep refusing the AI tools unless there's a fair deal, even if that costs me some work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but it's still a loss. It feels like being told your street will be knocked down in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Noor change any plans with ten years ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the kids question. We'd talked about maybe in five years, and I think we'd hold off until we know whose job survives. That sounds bleak, but it's how I'd think it through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd refuse the tools. Is there any point where you'd give in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came down to the rent, yes, I'd use them, I'm not a saint. But I'd do it with my eyes open and I'd keep printing by hand. I'd rather be the person who still knows how to print by hand, when everyone else has forgotten.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a real chance to make the rules now.
I'd want **artists** at the table when those rules get written.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when it lands, young enough to build a second trade.
I'd still lose design, but I wouldn't be **starting from nothing**.
do: Build **printing and sign painting** on the side with real clients over several years.
Save up to **six months** and look at a **shared studio** with two friends.
Hold off on **starting a family** until we know whose job survives.
feel: **Calmer**, but still a loss, like hearing your street gets knocked down in ten years.
S4.quote: I'd rather be the person who still knows how to print by hand, when everyone else has forgotten.
fieldNote: Ten years moves her from alarmed to **anxious**, because she sees time to build a **second trade**.
Her line on AI tools **softens** under rent pressure, which she admits openly.
She links the timeline to **family plans**, delaying children until jobs are clearer.

steps.text: Take paid sign-painting jobs alongside her studio work
Grow savings to six months of rent and bills
Split rent on a shared print studio with two friends
Delay trying for children until both jobs look clearer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because two years isn't enough to learn a new trade, and design is almost all thinking work. What would help is money while you retrain, paid for by the companies doing the replacing. And proper credit and payment for artists whose work these tools learned from.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we lose. If every poster for every small theatre comes out of the same machine, the city starts to look the same. Nobody's counting that, and I think somebody should.

headlineQuote: If every poster for every small theatre comes out of the same machine, the city starts to look the same.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old designer** at a six-person agency making posters for theatres, galleries and charities.
She has **never used AI tools** and refuses on principle, because she sees them as built on artists' unpaid work.
She lives with her **girlfriend**, a night-shift nurse, and has about **four months** of savings.
Across the scenarios she expects her **design job to end**, and plans a turn to hand printing and sign painting.
Her answers lean on **unions and public policy**, from a retraining fund to a wage for displaced workers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because two years is too short to learn a new trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Money while retraining**, paid for by the companies that replace workers.
Proper **credit and payment** for artists whose work trained the tools.
